MR MACDONALD-MINISTERIAL, STATEMENTS RESPECTING NORTHUMBERLAND CAUSEWAY CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising from a series of misleading statements and misrepresentation made in this house by members of the government with respect to a major governmental undertaking, the Northumberland strait causeway. I believe my question of privilege can be fully documented from the records of this house over the last year and a half.
Shortly after this first session of parliament began I put a question on the order paper concerning the expected date of completion of the Prince Edward Island causeway. The reply of the Minister of Public Works is found at page 1148 of Hansard, and reads as follows:
It is impossible at this early date to forecast accurately when a project of this magnitude and complexity will be completed. However, with maximum progress this project could be completed in late 1970.
One might say the minister protected himself well in that statement. However, outside of the house he went on record as announcing and in fact reiterating the earlier announcement of the proposed completion date of 1970. As if to underline the fact the government had indeed committed itself to a completion date late in 1970 the Minister of Finance, as recorded in his budget speech at page 3382 of Hansard, referred to one of the items for deferment or for rescheduling as follows:
A readjustment of the timetable for the next phase of the Northumberland causeway project in order to minimize the pressures on the peak summertime employment market and maximize winter employment possibilities;
Later the hon. member for Kings (Mr. McQuaid) sought assurance from the Prime Minister with regard to the completion of the causeway. The reply he received is recorded at page 3860 of Hansard:
-I can assure him there will be no delay in the completion of the project.
At an even later date, on April 19, a question was asked again by the hon. member for Queens of the Minister of Public Works who replied, as recorded on page 4030 of Hansard: I hasten to assure the hon. member that the Northumberland strait causeway is not being delayed in any way. The completion date is unchanged. It remains as it was when stated in the first announcement.
Later on the same day he said:
The new schedule provides for uninterrupted effort to build the P.E.I. approach to the proposed nine mile crossing.
After all these statements assuring us of this completion date, last Friday afternoon in this house the Minister of Transport was able to say, as reported on page 626 of Hansard:
The government has never at any time been so imprudent as to suggest a precise date for the completion.
I suggest, in the first instance, that there has been a very careful plan on the part of the government to mislead the members of this house as to whether in fact there will be completion of this important transportation link by late 1970. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not regard this as the basis of my question of privilege for it relates, in fact, to the very design and construction of the project itself. In January of this year, as will be found recorded on page 12408, I asked the Minister of Public Works, in the light of rumours of a possible report by O. J. McCulloch, whether indeed there would be design changes in the causeway. The minister replied on that date: Mr. Speaker, none are contemplated.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
One might allow the minister some latitude at this point, Mr. Speaker; after all that was some months ago, and the government cannot be expected to be that accurate even after assessing this problem for three or four years. But this past month, on May 18, I again asked the minister whether he could tell the house when we might expect the awarding of the major contract called for March 31 so the next section could be gotten under way. In the first instance the minister was unable to reply, but in the second instance I put a supplementary question to him and asked whether the minister would assure the house that within the next two weeks we would
June 1, 1967

Prince Edward Island Causeway have an announcement of the awarding of the contract. The minister's reply, as reported at page 345 of Hansard, was as follows:
I expect we will have it within the next two weeks, Mr. Speaker.
Those two weeks have now come and gone, Mr. Speaker, and we have had no word on the awarding of this contract. Rather we have had word of a deferment. As my most conclusive argument, Mr. Speaker, I refer to Hansard for May 23, on which day I asked the minister once more whether any action had been taken by the government to defer or redesign this project. In a supplementary question I asked him whether the government was planning to defer this project, and the minister answered with a categorical "No, Mr. Speaker".
Some months ago a report was published in our local paper under the headline "Are our Islanders being taken for a toboggan ride?" I think the answer to that question today is a categorical "yes" because of the way in which this government through the past months has deliberately misled the members of this house and the people of Prince Edward Island with regard to this worth-while and important project.

subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAYCOMMENTARY BY MR. MCCULLOCH

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAYCOMMENTARY BY MR. MCCULLOCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Queens asked me whether the Department of Public Works had completed its examination of the commentary by Mr. O. J. McCulloch on the Northumberland strait crossing and whether Mr. McCulloch's services would be utilized in our reassessment of the design of the crossing. I indicated that no consideration is being given to obtaining Mr. McCulloch's services but that I would make a statement on motions today as to the commentary and revised commentary sent to the department by Mr. McCulloch.
The contention of Mr. McCulloch is that the crossing should be built in precisely the way the Canso causeway was built, that is that it should be a solid causeway. In all his proposals Mr. McCulloch has assumed conditions existing as they were at Canso. This is patently not the case. The Canso causeway crossed a strait approximately three quarters of a mile long where changes in tidal conditions were not significant although there were some damage claims. The project we are now considering is a nine mile crossing located approximately in the middle of a 100 mile reach of the Northumberland strait.
While investigating the feasibility of the Northumberland crossing the government had a complete tidal study made. An analysis of this tidal study was made by the Liverpool Observatory and Tidal Institute of England to predict the results of placing a restriction in the strait. The results of their study, confirmed by subsequent model studies, indicated that a full causeway would change the tidal regimes throughout the strait. The changes would be very significant. At the crossing site the average tidal range at present is 7i feet, whereas complete closure would increase the tidal range by 5| feet on the east side and 2J feet on the west side. To these changes in tidal ranges it is necessary to add the effects of storm surges and wind setup. On the other hand, if a crossing is designed to provide a minimum of 35 per cent of the cross-section open to flow, changes in the present water level conditions throughout the strait are not significantly altered.

In considering these facts the government had surveys made to consider the direct costs which might arise as a result of property damage, flooding effects on roads, bridges, marine structures and dredging, if water levels were changed. These, at 1959 values, were estimated at $23 million. What these costs would be in 1967 is problematical, and to evaluate them would involve a completely new assessment of lands, roads and bridges, marine structures and development since the survey of 1958-59. What was impossible to forecast or estimate, however, was the extent of potential damage to individuals or corporations located in and using the strait for marine purposes where their facilities and potential development would be affected by changes in water levels. Added to this was the potential of disturbing the existing conditions as they may affect the fisheries industry which would involve not only changes in depth but also water temperature conditions and water flow generally.
Having regard to all these factors the government wished to maintain, in so far as possible, the existing tidal regime, and this is still our judgment. This is particularly so when we have carried our engineering investigations to such an extent that we can provide an opening which will maintain the tidal regime. We can make provision for ice, and we are proceeding on this basis and do not accept the alternative of a solid causeway.

Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to discuss such a technical statement without the text before me, and I am very much a layman in this field. However, Mr. Speaker, I am impressed by the assurance with which the minister seems to reject the suggestions of Mr. McCulloch. The minister described Mr. McCulloch's suggestion as a commentary. I have a copy of Mr. McCulloch's report before me, and it seems a little more ample than a mere commentary.
Considering the degree to which the department has had to admit errors and miscalculations I wonder at the presumption with which it is able to cast aside so summarily the suggestions made by Mr. McCulloch. Indeed I am wondering why in recent years Mr. McCulloch's submissions have not been more carefully studied. Although I hold no brief for Mr. McCulloch's suggestions I think it is fair to say he took stock of the resultant damage to the coasts of both provinces which would ensue from the building of a solid causeway-

-and in his calculations he estimated the cost of remedial steps. The minister interjects from his seat that he did not. I contend he did, and have the document before me. Mr. McCulloch did take this into consideration. Considering the whole causeway crossing project it would also appear to me that the very phase which yesterday was reported to be under reassessment, and for which contracts were not awarded, is the causeway section on the New Brunswick side which would be built and could be built if Mr. McCulloch's plans were adopted. Therefore, I and many people in Prince Edward Island are still possessed of a feeling of uneasiness about this whole project, and I am not convinced that much has been done to dissipate that uneasiness by casting aside the practical suggestions made by Mr. McCulloch.
Since the government seems to have to reappraise so much, and this despite the fact that yesterday in an answer given to the hon. member for Cumberland it was revealed that $1J million had been spent on research, I would commend to the government that in its reappraisal it should have closer consultation with Mr. McCulloch, who has at least produced a plan that is economically feasible according to his figures. speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau for the second reading of Bill No. S-6, to revise and consolidate the Interpretation Act and amendments thereto, and to effect certain consequential amendments to the Canada Evidence Act and the Bills of Exchange Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Perhaps I should remind the house that when this matter was debated a few days ago the Minister of Justice had the floor at the time and was closing the debate.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I had in fact concluded my remarks but a few questions were asked, notably by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and I said that before finally closing the debate I would endeavour to answer them to his satisfaction.
Among other questions the hon. member asked to what extent the bill we are now considering differs from the bill which last March was referred back to the house by the standing committee on justice and legal affairs, and to what extent these changes appear in the bill now before us. I pointed out that there were four extremely minor changes. He asked me whether I could give him a list of them, and I have one here. Although the hon. member is not here at present, I am sure he and other hon. members would agree if I indicate these changes when we reach the particular clauses in which they appear. These changes are of a minor nature; for instance, a word is changed from the plural to the singular. I have the list with me now, but I suggest that perhaps this would be more expeditious.
The other matter was the question of the definition of "regulation". The hon. member asked whether I would point out in the bill the clauses where the word "regulation" appears. In fact there are only three clauses in which this word appears. They are to be found on page 8 of Bill S-6, in clause 23 (2); page 17, clause 33(1) (b); and page 19, clause 37 (g).

June 1, 1967
Interpretation Act
I should like to point out that the bill uses the word "enactment" on practically every page, and sometimes several times on the page. If we look at section 2 of the Interpretation Act we see that "enactment" includes a regulation. Therefore every time the word "enactment" or "enact" appears in a section it includes a reference to regulation. In that sense, therefore, although the word "regulation" does not appear in a great many places, it is really included in the word "enact" which does appear frequently. That is why it was found useful in clause 2 (1) (e) to define the word "regulation" in a general way which will apply to all sections of this act.
Incidentally, in rereading what I said the other night I noticed that I indicated that since "regulation" is defined in the bill it would tend to apply to all other statutes. Of course this is not necessarily so. Clause 2 (1) (e) gives the definition of "regulation". When it appears in other acts it will have the particular meaning ascribed to it in the context or in the definition in that particular act. This is the factual answer to the question put to me by the hon. member.
When we reach the particular clauses the hon. member may want to discuss the interpretation we give to these words, but 1 think he was perfectly justified in asking me to point out the usefulness of defining "regulation". I repeat, the usefulness of defining it is that it appears in the word "enactment" in a great number of clauses of this bill.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The third question, which is more substantive, was asked by the hon. member and was then taken up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Subsequently it was taken up by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). I was asked to give examples of cases where a regulation, in this general sense, could be made under the authority of the governor in council and not by virtue of a statute. I answered in a general way that there would be many such cases where the governor in council acts by virtue of the royal prerogative, which of course is the most obvious one.
The hon. member asked me for some other examples. I shall give a few today in the hope this will help the discussion. For instance, Mr. Speaker, when an ambassador is appointed under the Great Seal, this is done by the governor in council but not by virtue of any statute. This action is taken under a prerogative which, from time immemorial, has belonged to the king or queen under our form

of government and has come down by way of prerogative to the governor in council who exercises the executive power. This is an example of a prerogative where an action is taken without the authority of a specific statute.
Another example is when the governor in council appoints a person as a queen's counsel or indeed confers upon him some other honour. These actions are not taken under the authority of any particular statute. It is a matter of the royal prerogative as it has been understood in this country.
If I may digress slightly, Mr. Speaker, I do want to remind hon. members that I am not at this time asking for the extension or indeed the restriction of the exercise of the prerogative. As I indicated the other night, perhaps this would be an interesting debate at some other time. Perhaps it might be useful if some members want to express their opinion on the utility of the restriction of the prerogative by statute. I do not want to enter into such a debate at this time. I merely want to remind hon. members that an interpretation act is certainly not the place to discuss this subject. An interpretation act merely tells us how certain words, certain sections of statutes or regulations should be interpreted. Such an act does not tend to create substantive law. Once again I say I do not believe the whole issue of the prerogative should be debated at this time.
I should like to give another example of action taken or regulations made under the authority of the governor in council but not authorized by statute. I cite the proclamation of a day to be observed, either in part or in totality, as a public holiday. There is no statute of which I know which authorizes the governor in council to do that. As an employer the government can do this. The government can decide to issue some rule, regulation, bylaw, whatever it is called in this definition, to the effect that today the employees can go home at three 'clock in the afternoon. This action is not taken under the authority of a statute. If such an order is given granting a holiday or part holiday or appointing a Queen's Counsel, it may be useful to know when the order takes effect. The Interpretation Act will permit us to say, if a day is mentioned, that it will begin on that day or, if an hour is mentioned, it will begin at that particular hour. The Interpretation Act will tell us whether it should be understood in terms of standard time or what.
June 1. 1967

These are a few examples. There are quite a few others which I could give if the discussion is continued. I do not want to prolong this debate. I believe I have given sufficient examples to indicate that the Interpretation Act is not increasing the government's power to issue regulations in the general sense. The intention of this bill is to show what the words mean, how they shall be interpreted in a case where the power does exist. However, Mr. Speaker, if the power does not exist under some statute or under some prerogative, then the Interpretation Act cannot create such power. If the power does exist under an act or under a prerogative, then the Interpretation Act tells us how the words we find in that act or regulation shall be interpreted. I feel I have covered the points which were raised in the first instance by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and I suggest we move to the clause by clause study of the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hesitated in rising because I thought other hon. members were going to explore further the matter of the definition of regulations. If that is not the case, I should like to raise one matter, not in any formal way which would require a decision but just to express a thought about what I feel is a fiction rather than a fact. Somewhere along the line, even though the Minister of Justice did not feel it appropriate to debate some of these matters in any depth, I submit we must make a determination on the matters before us.
I should like to refer to paragraph (e) of clause 2 which relates to the governor in council. In order to understand what governor in council means, we have to look at clause 28 on page 12 of the bill. I should like to read it:
"Governor in Council" or "Governor General In Council" means the Governor General of Canada, or person administering the government of Canada for the time being, acting by and with the advice of, or by and with the advice and consent of, or in conjunction with the Queen's Privy Council for Canada;
This is a bit of fiction, really. When we are talking about the governor in council we are talking about the cabinet because we know that the governor general's office has no real authority attached to it. We know that the
Interpretation Act
authority which the monarch at one time exercised has been removed and rests in the hands of the prime minister and the other ministers. In view of all these definitions about who the governor in council is and what is the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, I would suggest that at some stage in our discussions we should dispense with them because in fact they are fiction.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I consulted my seatmate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as to his understanding of what the Queen's Privy Council for Canada is and he substantiated what I understood it to be, that it embraces quite a number of people among whom are, of course, the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Coldwell who for many years was leader of the C.C.F. party in Canada, and quite a number of others.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
In fact, most of the front benchers in the Conservative ranks, leadership candidates and others. They are all included in the definition of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada. However, I am sure that none of them is included in the definition of the governor in council because none of them, certainly those out of office, is consulted or invited to meetings of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada. The Governor General of Canada, in doing some of the things that is required of the governor in council, does not seek the advice of the privy council or ask for their consent or even work in conjunction with them.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, we should not perpetuate an archaic fiction of this sort in any law, whether it be the Interpretation Act or any other act. I would far sooner see us spell out what we are talking about here. When we are talking about the governor in council we are referring to the Governor General and the members of the federal cabinet, and that is all we are referring to. We do not include sundry other people who were at one time members of a cabinet or have been given honorary recognition by the title of "a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council for Canada". We should not perpetuate this fiction by continuing it in this act.
I understood the Minister of Justice in his closing remarks on second reading stage to say that he did not think that this was the place to become involved in any detail in the question of prerogatives. Yet, Mr. Chairman,

June 1, 1967
Interpretation Act
we are involved in them. The matter was raised by the hon. member for Peace River and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who inquired what was meant by regulation. The Minister of Justice spent some time in explaining the reasoning behind doing things in this way.
I am wondering whether the minister of Justice has had any further thoughts about this question. For my sake I would far sooner see the phrase "governor in council" eliminated so that the Governor General is looked upon purely as a person with a title but with no authority in fact. I submit we should spell out in our law just what it is we are talking about when we talk of somebody having the authority to promulgate regulations, awards, proclamations, or whatever it is according to the definition here. If we define this authority as the cabinet or as the council of ministers, then let us say so instead of maintaining in the law something that is not the case in fact purely because we want to hang on to some piece of history which really has no present day value to us.
In this regard I am talking, of course, about clause 28, but we have to think about that clause in conjunction with clause 2. Certainly I think we should spell out what we mean by the Queen's Privy Council for Canada. We should say that it does not include everyone who happens to hold that title. If it is to include everybody who happens to hold that title, the Leader of the Opposition and his former cabinet colleagues should be invited to sit with the council when it makes decisions.
I am sure the minister would be surprised at the benefits that might flow from this sort of multi-party approach to government decision making. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for Skeena has raised a very interesting question of constitutional law. I would go so far as to say that he is more than 99 per cent right in saying that when we talk of the governor in council we are in fact talking about cabinet. There are cases where all privy councillors can be summoned, either by the Queen or by the Governor General, though the chances are that this would be mainly for honorific reasons. Nevertheless this body does exist in fact. When we talk about the cabinet the hon. member is quite right, we are talking about a portion of the privy council. In reality, I think that under our constitution we call it the committee of the privy council.
I would agree with the hon. member that the term used here is archaic. If the hon. member wishes to indicate once again that this is the time to withdraw such archaic expressions from our law, I would explain to him why I believe that under our constitution as it is written in the British North America Act the expression "cabinet" does not appear. Nor, indeed, do many of the other institutions of our parliamentary form of government exist under our written constitution. For instance, I do not think you will find in the B.N.A. Act any reference to the word "party". Yet everybody knows what an important part parties play in the formulation of our laws and the workings of our parliamentary system of government.
The point raised by the hon. member for Skeena was that we should remove these archaic expressions when we can. Here again I agree with him, but I would point out to him the consequences of removing this expression in such a statute as this. It would mean that we would, in a sense, be saying that regulations can be made by an instrument of state-cabinet-which in a technical sense under our constitution does not exist. To put that another way, Mr. Chairman, under our constitution as it is written the executive arm of government is controlled by the governor in council, not by cabinet. If we were, therefore, in some particular statute denying the

June 1, 1967

reality of the governor in council and replacing "governor in council" with the word "cabinet", we would be using a word which does not have any formal existence in our written constitution.
[DOT] (3.50 p.m.)
Obviously the hon. member may well reply that our constitution is much more than what is written in the British North America Act and that is correct. The constitution of Canada is only partly written, in much the same way as the constitution of the United Kingdom is partly written but to an even smaller degree. The constitution of the United Kingdom appears in a certain number of statutes but the overwhelming part of it exists really in a fiction which is accepted by the people of the United Kingdom and which allows them to accept their parliamentary way of government.
In Canada, because we were creating a federal form of government and because we had to write a constitution at least to the extent that we were dividing powers between the regional and central government, we added other factors in our constitution which are archaic not only now but were archaic when they were written. We perpetrated these fictions, these expressions, because they were understood by the people of Canada to refer to a parliamentary form of government upon which we were modelling ours. Indeed, the preamble to the British North America Act indicates that the parliament of Canada is based largely on the kind of parliamentary system which then existed in the United Kingdom. We were doing at that time, therefore, the only logical thing we could do.
The next point then is: Should we change this constitution? The hon. member's party and the government party have some differences of opinion on this subject, not so much as to the idea of changing the constitution, perhaps but as to the timing of this change. To use the kind of jocular note that the hon. member used, I suggest that even in his party there is some disagreement about the kind of change which would be required in the present constitution. I can only suggest to the hon. member that this is not the occasion, under the guise of the Interpretation Act, to try to bring all parties in this house and all hon. members into agreement as to what the constitution should be.
One of the easiest matters upon which we could all agree and which could be carried out would be to remove some archaic expressions in the constitution. This, I suppose, will 27053-531
Interpretation Act
be done when next we revise or rewrite the constitution. The hon. member knows that it has always been my feeling that this particular kind of symbolic issue is not the most urgent kind of issue. I feel that if we were to reopen the constitution of Canada and begin to discuss with each other or even to fight over a purely symbolic issue, we might soon find that it would have been wiser to leave the symbols alone when they were working well. I do not think that the hon. member will disagree with me if I suggest that when we talk of the governor in council we really mean a committee of that council called "cabinet", and that the fiction is working reasonably well. That being so, I suggest that this afternoon we continue using that fiction at least until this bill has been passed.

Mr. Chairman, the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena is indeed raised at the right place. The amendment which would achieve the object he seeks would be very simple. It would consist of deleting the clause completely. He is right. If we did it here it would apply to the whole of our statute law and it would abolish a very ancient principle of English common law according to which the crown is not bound by a statute unless it is specifically mentioned in the statute. I understand that the hon. member wishes to achieve this result, and this could be done simply by deleting this particular clause.
The only question I will put to the hon. member is whether or not it would be proper to do away with this very ancient principle in order to achieve the particular result for which he is hoping. Although this is only a wild guess, I suggest that we would not only be doing away with an ancient principle but with a very important one both in common law and in statute law, one which is a very important cornerstone of our constitution, because the deletion of this clause might be interpreted as an intention expressed by parliament to bind the crown under every statute. For instance, when laws are passed concerning taxation, tariffs or even provisions under the criminal law stating that no person shall do such and such, this would mean that these laws also bind the crown.
I am afraid that the effect which we would achieve would be of much greater consequence than the hon. member suspects. There are other ways of achieving the result he seeks, which I suggest in particular cases is a desirable objective. One is for parliament to use the reverse rule and to say in a statute that it binds the crown. If this was not done

June 1, 1967
Interpretation Act
at the time the statute was passed, it is always open to parliament to express its intention to bind the crown under a particular statute. However, quite frankly I feel that to decide all at once that all statutes would be binding on the crown, without re-examining all our statutes thoroughly and completely, would be reckless at this time. I am afraid that if we did this we would find that the crown in right of Canada and indeed in right of the provinces would have its powers altered in a very drastic way. I suggest that if the hon. member wants to achieve the aim he is seeking, he can do it much more safely and efficiently by introducing an amendment to that effect in a particular statute rather than by attempting to do it through the Interpretation Act.

Subclause 17 of clause 28 gives the definition of "holiday". In the main part of the subclause the following days are listed as holidays: Sunday, New Year's Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Christmas Day, the Queen's birthday, or the day fixed by proclamation for the celebration of the birthday of the reigning sovereign, Victoria Day, Dominion Day, the first Monday in September, designated' Labour Day, Remembrance Day, and any day appointed by proclamation to be observed as a day of prayer or mourning or .as a day of public rejoicing or thanksgiving, :and so on. The "so on" refers to a couple of :subclauses relating to holidays proclaimed in a province, or in a city, town or municipality.
My concern at this time relates to certain of these specific holidays, the list of which I have just read. As hon. members know, some of these holidays fall on days which are fixed by tradition in such a way that we would not think of moving them one way or the other. Though Easter itself is a movable feast, Good Friday always falls, of course, on the Friday before Easter Sunday and Easter Monday is always on the Monday after Easter Sunday. Labour Day is always celebrated on the first Monday in September. Victoria Day is the day on which we celebrate the birthday of the reigning sovereign and we have declared by statute that this falls on the Monday preceding May 24, not on May 24 itself unless that day is a Monday.
Hon. members are probably aware by now of the point I am about to make, because I have asked questions about this on one or two occasions in recent weeks, namely, the somewhat strange situation which arises because the hundredth birthday of this nation, Dominion Day, 1967, falls on a Saturday, a day which is already a day off for many people. The result is that for a great many Canadians there will be no holiday in terms of a day off

work. My request to the Prime Minister was that because Dominion Day falls on a Saturday this year arrangements should be made for Monday, July 3, also to be a holiday.
I wish to make it clear that I was not suggesting and do not now suggest that Monday, July 3, should be Dominion Day rather than the Saturday, July 1. But 1 maintain that if there is any excuse at all for a long week end there should be a long week end in celebration of the hundredth birthday of this nation.
A few days ago an hon. member of this house brought in a bill to change the name of Dominion Day to "Canada Day" and at the same time to provide that it be celebrated always on the first Monday in July. I am very sympathetic toward the first part of his bill, the proposal that the name should be changed, but I am not yet persuaded that it would be a good idea to have it always on Monday because there is something traditional, almost sacred, about the first day of July, and I think that should be the date.
We already provide by statute that if July 1 falls on a Sunday, July 2 shall be a legal holiday. There are several laws of that kind in our statutes. That kind of provision originated, of course, in the days of the six day work week. The five day week is now reasonably general and I submit that the same motives as those which led to the decision that a holiday falling on a Sunday should result in a public holiday on the following Monday should now be applied here and that a holiday which falls on a Saturday should be followed by a legal holiday on the Monday immediately thereafter.
I asked the Prime Minister about this on Thursday, May 18, at which time he said he would look into the matter. I asked him about it again on Friday, May 26, as reported in Hansard at page 603, and perhaps I might read the right hon. gentleman's reply on that occasion. These are the Prime Minister's words:
I have been looking into the matter. It seems quite clear that in so far as the public service of Canada is concerned the subject is covered by the public service terms and conditions of employment regulations, which became effective in March of this year. In accordance with these regulations a great majority of public servants will get a holiday on July 3. So far as parliament is concerned, it will of course be the responsibility of the house to decide whether or not to sit on that day. There has been some discussion on that score among the house leaders.
There is one more sentence 1 should like to quote from the Prime Minister's reply. It

I hope, rather, that he was conscious of the fact that Bill S-6 was before parliament and that we would have an opportunity to amend this legislation so as to provide that the Monday following a holiday which falls on a Saturday should also be a holiday.

Yes, I think the arithmetic of the hon. member for Halifax is correct. On one day out of every two years we would get a holiday falling on a Saturday which by the terms of my amendment would be recognized as the holiday but it would be followed by the Monday thereafter also being a holiday.
I offer this amendment as the answer to the plea made by the Prime Minister. On Friday morning, May 26, the Prime Minister seemed anxious to meet my request. He said that the civil service will get the day off but that as for parliament it is up to parliament itself. He added that as for the country generally it could only be done by legislation. My first thought was to produce a private member's bill, but the chance of getting it passed by July 1 would be nil. Then I realized we had this legislation before parliament and we could do it under this legislation.
To place the matter formally before the committee I move:
That subclause (17) of clause 28 of Bill S-6 be amended by inserting, on page 12, in line 33, immediately after the words "Remembrance Day;" the following words:
"any Monday that follows immediately after any of the foregoing holidays when any such holiday falls on a Saturday;"
If I may, I would like to read the subclause as it would then appear:
(17) "holiday" means any of the following days, namely, Sunday; New Year's Day; Good Friday; Easter Monday; Christmas Day; the birthday or the day fixed by proclamation for the celebration of the birthday of the reigning sovereign; Victoria Day; Dominion Day; the first Monday in September, designated Labour Day; Remembrance Day; any Monday that follows immediately after any of the foreogoing holidays when any such holiday falls on a Saturday; any day appointed by proclamation to be observed as a day of general prayer or mourning or as a day of public rejoicing or thanksgiving; and any of the following additional days-
I think my proposal really meets the wishes of members generally. I think it certainly would be in accord with the desire of the general public. Here we have the chance to see to it, since long week ends are a way of celebrating a holiday, that that is what we will have for our one hundredth birthday.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. I repeat once again the argument I seem to have repeated a great number of times since we began our discussion of this bill. I believe it is a mistake to use this act to achieve purposes which could be more rightly achieved in conformity with the intention of parliament by amending some other act.
June 1, 1967

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to an existing statute which says that when a certain holiday falls on a Sunday it shall be celebrated on the Monday. Surely this would be the proper place to introduce an amendment of this kind or indeed, as he indicated, by way of a private member's bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Before the hon. member feels too certain about what he says, I should like to point out to him that by introducing this kind of amendment in respect of this kind of a bill, in other words, by diverting the intention of the bill to achieve a particular purpose such as that which he hopes to achieve, he may in reality be defeating his own purpose. It is obvious, if this amendment should be accepted, that the hon. member would have introduced an amendment which does not apply to many other acts. For instance, it would not apply to civil service holidays because civil service holidays are not mentioned in this particular subclause and are not covered by the particular amendment which he suggests. Nor would it cover bank holidays which come under the Bills of Exchange Act. The other night he gave the example of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which sets out a number of holidays. These holidays would not be affected by this particular amendment.
These are examples of the various holidays which would not be affected by this amendment. They would, however, be affected by a more specific bill such as that which he suggested he could introduce or by amendment to legislation dealing with holidays falling on a Sunday.
The burden of my argument is that parliament should exercise as much logic as possible. An effort, through laudable intentions, to get bits of legislation into acts by the side door really does not fit into the framework of statute law when those acts are designated for other purposes. If we did this frequently we would have statutes which would be more complicated than they are and we would have members of the opposition complaining that it was not intended that legislation should be introduced by the back door into statutes which were adopted by parliament for a certain purpose.
To sum up, I should like to say that if this amendment were adopted it would perhaps achieve in the short run the effect of giving a holiday in this particular year on the
Interpretation Act
Monday, whatever date it is, but in tire long run it would be introducing a principle of confusion into our statute law. I suggest that once again we would be defeating the whole spirit of the Interpretation Act if we use it to change substantive legislation in this way. It would be back-door legislation and I do not agree with that procedure. If the government were prepared to agree to the intention the hon. member has in mind, I would suggest the way this should be done would be to proclaim that particular day as a holiday which, as I say, is a right the government possesses in a particular case by virtue of the royal prerogative. Surely if the government wanted to do that it would do it, and if it should not want to do it surely it should not be expected to accept that it should be done by back-door or side-door legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand the effect of the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is that whenever Christmas Day, New Year's Day, Dominion Day or November 11 fall on a Saturday these holidays should be celebrated on the following Monday. If I am correct in my calculation this would mean that probably only one day in every two years would be changed. There are four holidays involved and one would expect the ratio to be about four to seven so far as years are concerned. I find that July 1 and November 11 both fall on the same day of the year and Christmas and New Year's both fall on the same day of the year. In the case of Christmas Day and New Year's Day, they are one week apart; in the case of July 1 and November 11 they are several weeks apart.
I have some doubt whether I should support the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I have no very strong views concerning New Year's Day or Christmas Day, but I believe November 11 is not a day which should be celebrated as a day for a holiday but rather as a day for true remembrance no matter on what day of the week it should happen to fall.
For this very simple and perhaps emotional reason I have changed my position in the last ten minutes. I think we can handle any specific problems which arise. Perhaps the amendment could be introduced in a way which would be more acceptable so far as Christmas Day, New Year's Day and July 1 are concerned, but I would opt for the proclamation method rather than the statutory approach. For these reasons I shall vote against the amendment.

Interpretation Act

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three things I should like to say with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax and those of the Minister of Justice. First, I should like to make very clear again that in proposing these Monday holidays in the four cases mentioned I am not proposing-and the wording of my amendment would not accomplish this-that the holidays be on the Monday instead of the Saturday. This is not a proposal that July 3 be Dominion Day or that November 13 be Remembrance Day this year. It simply is a proposal that those days be days off as well as the Saturdays but that in both cases the day to be celebrated would still be the calendar day, July 1 for Dominon Day and November 11 for Remembrance Day.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Minister of Justice suggested that this should be done by a bill amending the particular statute rather than by amending the Interpretation Act. That is a very nice suggestion if the government is willing to give consideration to such a bill. I could put a bill on the order paper but it would be number 115 or 120, and its chances of being reached would be nil. That suggestion has meaning and significance only if the government is prepared to adopt the idea.
The minister also suggested this should be done, if it is to be done, by proclamation rather than by legislation. Yet the other day when I asked the Prime Minister about it a second time, so he would get the point quite clearly, he said it could only be done now by legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member should read the passage again, because it seems to me the Prime Minister was talking in a general way about having this done in the future. I said specifically that if we were proclaiming it we would have to do it each time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
If the minister reads the question and answer as they appear on page 603 of Hansard for Friday, May 26, I think he will see that I was talking about a situation created by the fact that July 1 this year falls on Saturday. I asked the Prime Minister particularly whether Monday, July 3, 1967, might be declared a legal holiday so that all Canadians would get at least one day off for the celebration of our hundredth birthday. In other words, my question related only to the celebration of our birthday this year. I

read the Prime Minister's reply in full a few moments ago, but in his final words he said:
So far as declaring an additional public holiday in the country is concerned, that can only be done now by legislation, I believe.
I do not wish to make a debating point of the fact that the Prime Minister said one thing and the Minister of Justice has now said another, but if further research gives weight to the fact that this can be done by proclamation or by royal prerogative, let us be told about that. Let us not have the Prime Minister refusing on the ground that this can only be done by legislation and the Minister of Justice saying that it can be done if the government wants to do so by some sort of royal prerogative.
The minister accused me of trying to effect something by back-door legislation, or trying to enact something substantial in a statute which is just supposed to spell out meanings. Let me point out to him that his own bill is doing the very thing he suggest we should not do. It does so in paragraphs (a) and (b) of subclause 17. This, is not only back-door legislation; it is blank-cheque legislation. It provides that any day the lieutenant-governor of a province may appoint shall become a holiday for that province, or any day a city, town or municipality appoints as a civic holiday shall be a holiday for that area or district. In other words, we do not even know what holidays we may be creating by this legislation. I suggest that to criticize my amendment on the ground the minister did, in view of these provisions, is to be inconsistent.
I contend that I have followed the style and the language of the section which says "holiday" means, and then spells out a number of days. My amendment does not change the fact that July 1, 1967, will be celebrated on Saturday, but I suggest it is perfectly proper for us to say that "holiday" in this case means that when a statutory holiday falls on a Saturday there shall also be a holiday on the following Monday.
The minister talked about what this may do in terms of pay for people who have to work, and that sort of thing. Even the statute which provides for a holiday on Dominion Day does not say anything about people getting time off or being paid if they work. The statute does not say anything in this regard about Remembrance Day or Victoria Day. It merely says that these are legal holidays. All I am asking in these four cases is that when the legal holiday falls on Saturday the following
June 1. 1967	COMMONS
Monday shall also be a legal holiday. I suggest this amendment is one that ought to be accepted.

The hon. member will know that in the subclause under discussion there are, indeed, some days which are religious feasts and which are holidays. The idea of giving the provinces, cities, towns or municipalities the right under the law-I should not say the right but the recognition that they can proclaim days that will become holidays within the meaning of the Interpretation Act is not giving them an opportunity, in the derogatory words used by the hon. member, to have a blank cheque. It is a recognition of the fact that there are religious days and ethnic days of importance to particular sections of the country. I think the minister has put this matter much more felicitously than I could. I was a member of the committee on procedure of the house which recommended to parliament that St. Jean Baptiste Day be a holiday. I have no difficulty in reconciling my feeling then and my feeling now to vote against this bid, so to speak. I felt then that we were members of a national parliament and as such I was very glad to recognize a holiday that meant a great deal to my colleagues here in parliament. If we begin legislating from this point of view for the provinces, so to speak, and that is what we would be doing, the holiday would lose its meaning.
Interpretation Act
Let us be frank about it. It would not be understood. I think this is really discrimination in reverse, which must be about as bad a form of discrimination as we can find. Furthermore, this holiday would have no application to most of the statutes of Canada but would only have application to the Interpretation Act and the occurrences that flow from it. As the minister pointed out, it does not affect the Labour Relations Act. Many other statutes do not incorporate this holiday. As a member of a national institution, fully conscious of what St. Jean Baptiste means to a good many of my colleagues, I can vote against this amendment.

I do not believe this is the type of measure under which to introduce this provision. I suggest it requires much greater consideration than we have given it today. It is a matter that the government can take under immediate consideration so that we get these holidays established on a national basis and not an ethnic group basis or on the basis of subdividing this country.

subtopic: COMMERCIAL SOLIDS PIPE LINE COMPANY

speakeroldname: Mr. Grant Deachman (lor Mr. Basford) moved
subtopic: COMMERCIAL SOLIDS PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-113, to incorporate Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-113 to
incorporate Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company stands in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), as will be seen from the face of the bill. As hon. members know, that "foolish" young man is headed toward the west coast this week end to give up the state of bachelorhood. As a consequence, at the moment I do not think he is very interested in this bill. But I think it shows how cool a cat the hon. member is when he carefully arranges to see that another member from the west coast takes this bill in his very necessary absence, necessary, that is, if he is going to lose his bachelorhood.
This bill deals with a company that wishes to operate a commercial solids pipe line. The pipelining of solids is not a new concept. The first commercial pipe line for transportation of solids was built in England, I understand in 1914 to move coal in water from the docks to a power plant less than 2,000 feet away. Short lines to move coal mine sludge were built in the United States as early as the 1920's. A 15-mile line to move 500,000 tons of salt a year in a saturated brine was built in Louisiana in the 1930's. Since then there have been some longer lines, notably the 108-mile pipe line between Georgetown and Cleveland to carry coal in water. There is also a 72-mile gilsonite line between Bonanza, Utah, and Grand Junction, Colorado.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
With few exceptions, most pipe lines transporting solids today suspend finely ground particles in a liquid, the mixture being called slurry. This slurry can be handled in somewhat the same way as other liquids. Another possible method is called capsuling. This involves casing the solids in rigid or flexible containers which are moved through the pipe line. In this field probably the most advanced research in the world has been carried out by the Alberta research council. The capsule method has not, however, yet been developed to the point where it may be used commercially for long distances. An association known as the Solids Pipe Line Research and Development Association has now been formed in Canada to further this research.
Private Bills
Another active group is the Pulp and Paper Research Institute of Canada which has pioneered the pipelining of wood chips. The University of Saskatchewan and the Saskatchewan research council are working on the pipelining of potash slurries.
In summary, a number of short solids pipe lines have been proven and are in operation today and many research groups and private company laboratories both in Canada and elsewhere are working on the technology required for pipelining a variety of commodities over long distances. It is appropriate that this effort continue and even increase and that Canada be a world leader in this technology, because no other nation has such great mineral resources located far from either tidewater or consuming markets. It is important to Canada that it should be able to move its landlocked mineral resources such as coal, potash, iron ore and sulphur to market at tariffs that do not prejudice it vis-a-vis other countries, the resources of most of which are near tidewater.
There is therefore a wide potential for a company in Canada devoted to transporting solids by pipe line. The company believes that if this application is granted Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company will be instrumental in constructing in Canada solids pipe lines of a much greater length and capacity than have ever been constructed anywhere else in the world.
So far I have dealt with the pipelining of solids and the objects of Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company in a general way. I now wish to describe to the house one particular project that is being planned for the proposed company. This is the construction of a pipe line for the transportation of sulphur in slurry form from the producing plants in Alberta to the Canadian west coast.
The world demand for sulphur has increased at a rate of more than 6 per cent annually during the past three years. In 1966 the free world produced 24.1 million tons and consumed over 24.9 million tons of this commodity. The 1970 free world production of sulphur is estimated at 31 million tons.
Concurrently with the expansion of the world markets for sulphur the production in the province of Alberta has increased at an enormous rate. Shell Canada Limited is the largest producer of sulphur in Canada. From the time that Shell Canada Limited started the first sulphur production from natural gas in Canada at Jumping Pound near Calgary in 1952-producing the total output of Alberta

June 1, 1967
Private Bills
from natural gas at that time of approximately 10,000 tons annually-the production of sulphur in Alberta has increased today to more than 1.8 million tons a year. Since 1952 many new plants have been constructed and others will be built in the future. It is anticipated that by 1970 the production in Alberta will have increased to approximately 3.2 million tons a year.
As sulphur has not so far been transported in solid form by pipe line on a commercial scale, research still has to be done before the company can be certain that this 750 mile pipe line from Alberta to the west coast is feasible. Since to a large extent the exact location of the route will be dependent on the outcome of the research and development program which is presently taking place and which will continue after incorporation of this company, no specific route can be designated, at this time. The company's confidence, however, can be measured by the large sums of money it has already spent and will spend in the next two years, if this bill is passed, in developing this research to maturity.
The advantage to Canada of a pipe line that would transport this sulphur to the nearest port at a steady and economical rate is readily apparent, and such a line would be the first of its kind in the world, thus putting Canada well in the lead in the pipelining of solids.
The transportation of sulphur by rail, the present method used to convey this product from Alberta to the coast, is costly and the availability of suitable rail cars to handle this movement is a problem. These costs have recently increased to the extent that Shell has paid approximately $2.24 million in 1966 for transportation and handling between these points. They anticipate that the industry will spend $21 million in freight and handling charges for offshore movements in 1970, based on present day arrangements. It is expected that the sulphur pipe line would reduce these costs, not only to Shell but also to other Alberta producers utilizing this pipe line, by approximately one third. The pipe line would be available on mutually acceptable terms to all producers in Alberta who can conveniently tie in with the line. For those using the line, participation in the equity of the company would also be available. The resultant savings and stability of transport cost would help appreciably to improve the competitiveness of Canadian producers in supplying world markets and would aid in the negotiation of long term contracts for sulphur sales without fear of spontaneous and non-controllable freight increases.

The sulphur pipe line project which they have under study envisages a 12 inch main line with smaller diameter feeder lines. It will likely originate near the city of Calgary around which a gathering system would be built to tie in plants in the immediate area. The main line would go south in order to pick up throughput as southern Alberta plants including Shell's large Waterton plant. The line would then enter the mountains at the Crowsnest pass and go west until it reached the coast in the Vancouver area. A preliminary survey has been made of the approximate route of the sulphur line and the company has detailed sketches which demonstrate this. For reasons already given, there is necessarily nothing final yet concerning the route of the pipe line.
The cost of the line is estimated at $50 million, and the company would expect this project to be financed as to 25 per cent by equity capital and as to the remainder by bonds, debentures or other form of borrowing. The authorized capital of Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company for which they have applied is $100 million. This means that if the sulphur pipe line is built with 25 per cent equity financing, there will be ample capitalization remaining for several other solids pipe lines in Canada of a like magnitude.
With regard to Shell Canada Limited, which will be the principal shareholder of the new company, 17.5 per cent of the voting power is in the hands of the public, and these shares are traded on stock exchanges in Canada. The remaining 82.5 per cent is held by another Canadian company called Shell Investments Limited, the head office of which is also in Toronto. Shell Investments is in turn wholly owned by a Netherlands company situated at The Hague and, finally, the ownership of that company is divided as to 60 per cent in the hands of the Royal Dutch Petroleum Company at The Hague, and as to 40 per cent in the hands of the Shell Transport and Trading Company in London, England.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
They are committing in excess of $1J million to slurry pipeline studies generally, of which $900,000 is directed to this sulphur effort. They are also confident that Canada can and should become the world leader in commercially adapting this technology to reduce overland transport costs for many other solid commodities including potash, wood chips, coal and iron ore, thus benefiting our
June 1, 1967

entire economy. The full weight of the technical ability of the Shell group is behind this application and they assure us that their efforts will be unstinting in forwarding the commercial adaptation of this technology.
I am not an expert on this subject. I am pinchhitting for my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. It is the practice of the house that bills dealing with pipe lines are referred to the committee on transport and communications so that their purpose and nature may be examined in the light of evidence from whatever witnesses hon. members may wish to call. A bill dealing with the new transport commission has already been before the house and before that committee. One of its clauses deals with the possible regulation of pipe lines by the commission.
I think it is likely that certain questions will arise in connection with the effect of government policy upon the proposals contained in this bill. There are all kinds of questions which hon. members might wish to ask in connection with this matter, answers to which could only come from the applicants themselves. My only request is that this bill be permitted to go to the committee where there would be an opportunity to examine it thoroughly. If there are hon. members present who object in principle to any aspect of the bill it is, of course, their privilege to kill it by talking it out when it comes back to this chamber. But I think it is of great importance to the development of Canada that we should lead the way in moving materials over long distances by new and more efficient forms of transportation.
For this reason I ask any member of the house who has reservations about these proposals not to carry them to the point of denying parliament an opportunity to consider whether this bill, either as it stands or with modifications, is not in the best interests of the economy of Canada. The only way in which we can find this out properly is by examining it in the standing committee on transport and communications. It is with this belief in mind that I place the bill before the house this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully appreciate the eloquence which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman), speaking as a substitute for the sponsor of the bill, has brought to bear upon this subject. I have some reservations though as to the efficacy of his last plea that our discussion of the principle of this bill, affecting a company which is making a
Private Bills
new venture in this field, should be limited to some 25 minutes. The question of a solids pipe line is one which deserves careful consideration, particularly since the hon. member has made this expose, telling us who is behind this bill and why it is wanted.
I think we should go further into the study of solids pipe lines and recognize that the basic work in this connection has been done, as indicated by the hon. member himself, through the research council of the province of Alberta, using not only funds provided by that province but in addition funds made available by the Department of Industry. The organizations taking part in this research are known as SPRDA-Solids Pipelines Research Development Association-and SPESA, standing for Solids Pipelines Economic Studies Association.
There was some difficulty attached to the federal legislation, which I thought was a lot of nonsense when I came into contact with it about a year ago, and since then I have had something to do with the working out of the details of the federal subsidies for the economic and development studies. The legislation and the regulations were not as clear as they should have been and in this particular case a fine line was drawn between the economic feasibility of solids pipe lines and the technical aspects-whether one could move solids via capsules. I thought this was a little too much. But there it was, and this artificial distinction had therefore to be drawn within the development associations.
Let us face it. Not only were government funds involved in these technical and economic studies but a consortium of about ten Canadian companies which are interested in transport was involved. The Canadian National Railways has an interest in SPRDA. So have the C.P.R., Canadian oil companies, and other industries.
This is a matter which deserves far more attention than has yet been given to it. Perhaps the sponsors of this bill are endeavouring to capitalize on the research which has been carried out. I preface my remarks with those observations because I think we have to put this whole matter in context, and I hope that representatives of all parties in this house on the transport committee will go into the history of what has actually happened with regard to solids pipe lines research and consider where the potential benefits should reside.
What we are primarily talking about here is the transportation of sulphur from the

June 1, 1967
Private Bills
province of Alberta to the Pacific coast. The sponsor rightly said that this was the real objective of the Shell Oil Company. More power to that company. We are vitally interested in the cheaper transportation of sulphur to export markets. Members of this house would be doing a disservice to the economy of this country and to our export markets if they reacted in a negative way to proposals for the movement of sulphur in the cheapest possible manner. The market is highly competitive.
But it is not only sulphur that is involved. There is the question of iron ore pellets from northwestern Alberta. There are other types of solids which have just as much claim to the benefits of research in this field as has sulphur. I think we ought not to concentrate exclusively on this particular product but look at the over-all picture. It is for this reason that while in principle I would like to see this application go to the committee I should like the committee to undertake a much more extensive investigation of solids pipe line projects and studies and related economic studies.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I feel that persons from the research council of Alberta and other research organizations should be called to tell us where we are heading, to say whether this is going to be beneficial; and if it is going to be of national import then certainly the Canadian National Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and others concerned with transportation must be brought into the picture.
I have talked to officials of the research council of the province of Alberta who have been involved in this particular project, and they paint a most imaginative picture. I do not think we should grant an exclusive monopoly, tantamount to a hunting licence, to any one particular firm. At the moment I am rather taken with the development in my own province of the Alberta Gas Trunk Pipe Line, which is financed publicly, the shares being first offered to residents of Alberta and then to other Canadians. If this were done Canadians could benefit in the equity financing of similar enterprises, without great international corporations coming in, financed by their own banks and insurance companies, and acquiring the lion's share of the equities and profits.
As I say, I am much more disposed to consider the system used in the financing of the Alberta Gas Trunk Pipe Line, rather than the system used for the Interprovincial

Pipeline and other types of operations. Indeed I am much more taken with that system than with the idea of using the Canada Development Corporation.
If solids are going to be moved through a pipe line from the province of Saskatchewan, I believe the people of Saskatchewan should be given a chance to get in on the equity ground floor. If pulp and wood chips are to be moved by pipe line from the interior of British Columbia, likewise let the people of British Columbia have the first crack at it. I offer this as a suggestion to hon. members, but I must say I am glad to see that somebody has realized the economic importance and economic potential of a solids pipe line, based primarily on experience in other countries and also on research work done by public authorities in this country working on behalf of and in co-operation with private industry.
Having said that, I am quite prepared to see this bill go to committee but I certainly hope a great deal of study will be made along the lines I have suggested, rather than confined to the narrow ambit of the financing of this particular group and what they intend to do. We should use this opportunity to look into the whole prospect of solids pipe lines as a means of transportation. One of the biggest difficulties we find in marketing the products of this country is the immensely high cost of transportation. If the railways can benefit by participation in pipe lines, more power to them, because the country as a whole will ultimately benefit as a result of these developments. I personally am prepared to accept this bill in principle, but with the suggestions I have given.

He said: Mr. Speaker, through the courtesy of the Parliamentary Librarian I spent a few hours today browsing through the first budget speech presented to the House of Commons almost 100 years ago by Hon. John Rose, minister of finance. It gave me some consolation and encouragement to observe that Mr. Rose took a full afternoon and part of the evening to deliver his speech dealing with revenues and expenditures of less than $20 million, and that from time to time when he expressed his fear of wearying the house he was met with cries of "no, no". I promise not to repeat that performance this evening. I hope nevertheless for the same indulgence from hon. members.
Mr. Rose was an eloquent speaker and, on the occasion of this centennial budget, I should like to recall a few sentences from this first budget after confederation.
In viewing the facts-
Mr. Rose said:
-I think they point, under the blessing of a good Providence, to a certain and prosperous future before us. If we work together in harmony, if we endeavour to cement the Union, if we develop the varied and rich resources of the several provinces, we have the elements within us to build up a prosperous and powerful community. In Lower Canada we have a people frugal, industrious, and attached to the soil-not a nomadic, but a steady, contented people, well adapted for manufacturing pursuits; while in the West we have immense agricultural, and in the East equally important maritime resources. I am not an enthusiast, but I say that although we have a rigorous climate and many difficulties to combat, we have correspondingly hardy, energetic and thrifty population, and in the extent and variety of our resources we have as certain a promise of a good future as any country ever before enjoyed.

Now, Sir, I would not wish it to be supposed that, in calling attention to these indications of the future prosperity of the country, I am desirous that we should rush into undue expenditure.
